title: Meeting the teacher
hookLine: a private meeting where the student shows their understanding

lines: A HAND BELL IN THE SILENCE.
A LINE OUTSIDE A CLOSED DOOR.
cards: In the middle of a silent sesshin, one sound cuts through the hall: a small hand bell. A student rises from the cushion and waits in line outside a closed door.
When it's her turn, she goes in, bows, and sits down across from the teacher. Just the two of them; nobody else will hear what's said. She may have a few minutes.
She has to show what she understands, not explain it, not quote a book. Show it. Today's word is the name for that meeting: dokusan.

teach.b: First, the word. Dokusan is Japanese, often rendered as going alone to the teacher. Not as a class or a group.
Whatever you've been sitting with, you carry into that room yourself. Second, what happens inside differs by school. In Rinzai halls the meeting often turns on a koan.
The student presents a response, and the teacher may accept it, ask a question, or ring the bell to end the meeting, which means: go back and sit with it more.

teach.h: A KOAN, OR A TALK ABOUT PRACTICE.
teach.b: In Soto communities, dokusan is often a quieter conversation about practice: how the sitting is going, where the mind keeps getting stuck. Different shape, same doorway.
Third, seen, not read. Zen tradition describes itself as a teaching passed from one person to another, not only through books.
A teacher can't see your understanding in your notes. They see it in how you walk in, how you answer, whether you hesitate or hide behind a clever line. Fourth, your understanding, right now.

A lot of everyday talk about what people think happens at a safe distance: in text, in summary, after the fact. Dokusan asks for something rarer: your actual understanding, now, in front of someone who's paying attention.
Even being turned away is part of it. The bell rings, the student bows, and walks back to the cushion with the question still alive.

how: In Zen communities, students meet the teacher privately during retreats and regular sittings; in Rinzai practice the meeting often centers on the student's koan, while in Soto practice it is often a conversation about the student's sitting and life.

o: a private meeting where a Zen student shows their understanding
a written test on the sayings of the old Zen masters

s: dokusan is a group question-and-answer session
it's private: one student, one teacher, a closed door.
being sent back by the bell is a failure

the teacher looks for what you understand now, not what you've read.

games.q: you're in dokusan with your koan. you've prepared a clever answer from something you read. the teacher waits. what do you do?
o: show what you actually understand, even if it's 'I don't know.'
games.why: the meeting is for your actual understanding, right now. a teacher may see through a borrowed answer, and the bell may send you back to sit.

practice: Imagine a quiet room and someone across from you who simply asks: how is your practice, really?

Find one honest sentence, not the polished answer: maybe I keep starting and stopping, maybe I don't know what I'm doing, maybe one small thing that's going well. Then let it rest, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Dokusan. A private meeting between a Zen student and teacher, where the student shows their understanding, and the teacher meets it directly. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: dokusan, rendered 'going alone' to the teacher. some Rinzai communities call it sanzen.

carryVoice: Your line: face to face. In that room, understanding isn't explained or quoted; it's shown. Until tomorrow.

sources.work: Zen communal practice, Rinzai and Soto
